job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Rafael Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at seven with coffee and the job listings, usually the regional banks and insurers, since I'd like to stay near Lyon. By ten I'm on the phone or writing a cover letter. In the afternoon I help my uncle Gaston with the accounts for his garage, and on Wednesdays I run with my flatmate Hugo. I rent a room in Villeurbanne. I finished a finance degree in June with the top mark in my year, and I did internships at a regional bank and at an insurance broker. I'm engaged to a girl called Camille, who's a primary school teacher, and we want to marry next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected. New things always get oversold, and then people go back to work. I'd tell my uncle that the garage's books won't need a new system, and I'd tell Camille that our plans stay the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel reasonably good, since the market here still has openings. The one thing I'd carry privately is that we've set a wedding date and I don't have a job to match. That's a pressure with nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I do. Apply to six or seven places a week, call the insurance broker where I interned, and keep doing my uncle's books for a bit of cash. I'd also keep saving. I want a deposit for a flat with Camille within three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. I'm not scared. It's like having a car that's fine but making a strange noise, and you want to get it looked at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the one pressure in your life right now that has nothing to do with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding next summer and my lack of income. Camille says not to worry, her salary covers the basics. I'm raised to believe a man provides, and it nags me that I've got a wedding date and no payslip. My father says an honest job in time is better than a quick one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you would you talk to about the job search, and what would they say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father, who's a retired postal worker, and my priest, Father Luc, who's good at calming me down. My father says keep going. Father Luc says patience is a kind of work. I take both seriously, though I wish I could point to a payslip.

say: I'd say new things are **oversold** and then people go back to work.
I'd tell Camille our **plans stay the same**.
think: The pressure is that we've set a **wedding date** and I have no job.
The market still has **openings**, which keeps me reasonably hopeful.
do: Send **six or seven applications** a week and call the insurance broker where I interned.
Keep doing my uncle's **garage books** for cash.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, like a car making a strange noise.

fieldNote: His unease is the **wedding date**, not AI.

Leans on his father and the priest for calm.

steps.text: Send six or seven applications a week to regional banks and insurers
Call the insurance broker where he interned about openings
Keep doing his uncle's garage accounts for cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a change that needs to be handled by people who do their job honestly. I'd say firms should train young people and not just buy software. At church or with Hugo I'd say it too, though I'm not loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the entry-level jobs change. At the bank I mostly checked loan files and entered data, both easy for a program. The broker still needs people who sit with a family and explain insurance, and I think there's a place for me in that. But there'd be fewer places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for insurance broking and branch banking, where the work is with people. I'd use the tools, because I already use them now and then, and would use them more to keep up. I'd ask Gaston to introduce me to garage-owner friends who need advice, as a first small client list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I know the market will move, and I'm not sure the pace suits my wedding date. But I'm not frozen. I'd change if I see it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which entry-level tasks in your field would go first, and what does that do to a job like the one you want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Data entry, loan file checks, and routine reports. The advice, the handshake and the trust stay with people, I think. My old boss at the insurance broker says ninety percent of her clients want to hear a voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who graduated a year after you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to go where the customer's face still matters, and to use the new tools to do their job faster. And I'd tell them to find an older person in the firm who'll teach them, because a mentor is worth more than any course.

say: I'd say firms should **train young people**, not only buy software.
I'd say it **quietly**, at church and with my flatmate.
think: Loan checks and data entry are **easy for a program**.
Brokers still need people who **explain** insurance to families.
do: Aim for **insurance broking** and branch banking, where the work is with people.
Ask Gaston to introduce **garage owners** as a first client list.
feel: **Anxious**: the market may move faster than my wedding date allows.
S1.quote: My old boss at the insurance broker says ninety percent of her clients want to hear a voice.
fieldNote: He aims for **people-facing** finance work and a mentor.
Uses AI sometimes and would use it more once it's proven.
Links the pace of change to his wedding plans.

steps.text: Apply to insurance brokers and branch banking roles that deal with people
Practise with AI tools to speed up client paperwork
Ask Gaston to introduce garage-owner friends as first clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest thing in my life and nobody is ready for it. I'd say it's a time for family, for church, for honest work and for government to act. I'd say to Camille that we hold together whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be afraid. My whole degree, my fiancée's and my plan for a flat, all depend on a world that might disappear. If machines do all the thinking work, my first job isn't coming. We'd have to rely on Camille's teaching salary, and I'd hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move the wedding plan only if I had to. I'd keep the date but make it smaller. I'd ask my uncle for full-time work at the garage, where I'd learn the trade, and put my savings in a safe account. I'd also go to the town hall to ask what help exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. The speed means no time to build anything. I'd have sleepless nights and stubborn faith, both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what changes about how you spend the next few months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count my savings, which are enough for about eight months. I'd decide with Camille what to keep, and I'd hold off on the flat. I'd learn some hands-on skills at the garage, since robots for that come about three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your family the night this was confirmed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to Camille that we'd marry anyway, with fewer guests. I'd say to my father that I don't know what comes next, and he'd say we manage. I'd then go to church and ask for some strength.

say: I'd say it's the **biggest thing** in my life and nobody is ready.
I'd tell Camille we **hold together** whatever happens.
think: My first job isn't coming if machines do all **thinking work**.
We'd have to rely on **Camille's** salary, which I'd hate.
do: Keep the wedding date but make it **smaller**.
Ask my uncle for **full-time work** at the garage and ask the town hall about help.
feel: **Alarmed**: sleepless nights and stubborn faith at once.
S2.quote: I'd have sleepless nights and stubborn faith, both at once.
fieldNote: The **wedding and the flat** make the stakes personal.
Falls back on his uncle's garage and a **smaller wedding**.
Pride matters: he'd hate relying on his fiancée's pay.

steps.text: Keep the wedding date but cut the guest list
Ask his uncle for full-time work at the garage
Move savings into a safe account and hold off on the flat
Go to the town hall to ask what help exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, and families should use it. I'd say to my priest that we should help young people find work with their hands and hearts as well as heads. I'd tell friends to plan, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can get a first job and still get the wedding and a small flat. I'd likely have a few good years. Then the thinking jobs would change, and I'd be ready to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take the first decent offer, marry next summer, save for a smaller flat, and take a course in something hands-on or personal, like financial advice for families. I'd save about a third of my pay. And I'd keep helping my uncle, since that's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. I have time to build, which helps. I'd feel the clock and I'd feel it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years of warning, what would you do differently from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd have been scrambling. With five I could keep the flat plan. I'd buy a smaller one, though, not the one Camille loves, so we'd keep a cushion. She'd understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd stop doing, or start doing, that you wouldn't if it were sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop planning for a career and plan for a family. A job's a means. I'd think of insurance advice as the long-term work, because it needs a person. And I'd look at the garage as a second option.

say: I'd say five years is something and families should **use it**.
I'd tell friends to **plan**, not panic.
think: I can get a first job and still have the **wedding and a flat**.
After a few good years the thinking jobs would **change**.
do: Take the first decent offer, **marry next summer** and save for a smaller flat.
Take a course in **financial advice** for families and save a third of my pay.
feel: **Anxious** but not frozen: I'd feel the clock every day.
S3.quote: I'd stop planning for a career and plan for a family. A job's a means.
fieldNote: Five years let him keep the **wedding and flat**, but smaller.

steps.text: Take the first decent job offer and marry next summer
Save a third of every payslip towards a smaller flat
Take a course in financial advice for families
Buy a smaller flat than the one Camille prefers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare, and the wise thing is to be steady. I'd say the old values still count: honest work, family, community. I'd tell my future children to learn something with their hands and their hearts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel mostly fine. Ten years is a full start to a career, a family and a home. By 33 I'd have children, probably, and I'd think about their future more than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get a job in insurance, marry Camille next summer, buy a flat by 26 or 27, and have a first child. I'd learn the tools as they become normal and keep helping the garage. I'd also become the kind of adviser who knows families by name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. I have a plan, and the plan works in a decade. I'd say it's a gentle worry, in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you do with the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep an annual check on how things are going, with Camille. We'd talk about whether to save more or move. And I'd teach my children a trade skill, so they're not just reading screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having a decade make you feel safe, or does it just push the worry further off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade feels safe for me, but the ten years after that I'd worry about, for my children. I think that's what a father worries about.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** and the wise thing is to be steady.
I'd say honest work, **family** and community still count.
think: Ten years is a full start to a career, a family and a **home**.
By 33 I'd think about my children's **future** more than mine.
do: Get a job in insurance, marry Camille and **buy a flat** by 26 or 27.
Become an adviser who knows **families by name**.
feel: Mostly **calm**: a gentle worry in the back of my head.
S4.quote: A decade feels safe for me, but the ten years after that I'd worry about, for my children.
fieldNote: The decade lets him follow the **traditional path** of marriage, home and children.
His worry moves to his future **children**.
He plans yearly check-ins with Camille.

steps.text: Build a career in insurance advice and learn the tools as they spread
Buy a flat by 26 or 27 with Camille
Plan a first child once the flat is bought

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It leaves no time to marry, buy a place or build anything, and it hits the thing I want most, a family and a home. What would help is a clear plan from government, real support for young families, and employers who stay loyal to the people they hire. And I'd like to see more apprenticeships that lead to work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people think a young man in finance is only worried about money. The people I love are what I worry about. If they're alright, I can face most things.

headlineQuote: The people I love are what I worry about. If they're alright, I can face most things.
portrait: Rafael is 23, a **top graduate** in finance from Lyon, renting a room in Villeurbanne and engaged to Camille.
He is traditional, faith-minded and keen on **apprenticeships** and honest work.
He uses AI tools now and then and changes when something is proven.
His moods move from uneasy to **alarmed**, because a wedding and a flat ride on his first job.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, which leaves no time to marry, buy a place or build a family life.
whatWouldHelp: A clear government plan, **support for young families**, loyal employers and more apprenticeships.
